source: Binz and Schulz (2022) Reconstructing the Einstellung Effect
finding: Luchins 1942 re-analysed: main effect. Plain group used the long E-solution on C1/C2 far more than controls, who never did.
numbers: N=310 (155 plain, 155 control). E-solution on C1/C2: 128/155 = 0.83 plain vs 0/155 control (chi2=218.02, p<.001). C3/C4: 100/155 = 0.65 vs 0/155 (chi2=147.62). Effect weaker on C3/C4 than C1/C2 (0.83 vs 0.65, chi2=13.0).
limits: Data are transcribed from tables in the 1942 thesis; no individual data, no reaction times. Percentages only.
agent_relevance: Baseline: a repeated method gets reused even when a cheaper one exists. Fading over later items hints that set weakens with disconfirming trials.

source: Binz and Schulz (2022) Reconstructing the Einstellung Effect (from Luchins tables 1-5)
finding: The warning 'Don't be blind' reduced but did not remove the set.
numbers: DBB group N=153: E-solution on C1/C2 87/153 = 0.57 vs 0.83 plain (chi2=24.16, p<.001). On C3/C4 57/153 = 0.37 vs 0.65 plain. DBB still showed C1/C2 > C3/C4 (0.57 vs 0.37).
limits: So 'over half switched' holds on C3/C4 (63% not E), but on C1/C2 only 43% avoided E (vs 17% plain). A warning alone leaves a large share fixated.
agent_relevance: A bare reminder to not be blind helps partly. Our G1 uses a signal-triggered doubt, not a generic warning; a warning prompt alone would be a weak lever.

source: Binz and Schulz (2022) (Luchins tables 12-13)
finding: Dose effect: more training problems gave a stronger set.
limits: Even two training problems gave 73% E use. Students from the New York area. Original data, not an independent replication.
agent_relevance: Repeating one strategy in context (few-shot examples, the agent's own earlier steps) should raise rigidity with the count of repeats. Cap repeated same-method examples.

source: Binz and Schulz (2022) (Luchins alternating condition)
finding: Alternating (interleaved) E and D training problems nearly removed the set.
numbers: Alternating group: 20/124 (0.16) used E on C1/C2 vs 97/121 (0.80) with plain blocked training; chi2=100.65, p<.001.
limits: Large effect (about 64 points). Single source (Luchins), no modern replication found.
agent_relevance: Strongest intervention found: vary the method across practice items. For the agent: mix example solution types in the prompt, never block one method.

source: Binz and Schulz (2022) (Luchins tables 28-30)
finding: Time pressure raised the set.
limits: Time pressure raised E use by 44 points on C3/C4. Stress effect confirmed in the reconstructed data.
agent_relevance: A tight token or time budget should push the agent toward the habitual route. Do not squeeze the check step (S4/S6) when the budget is low.

source: Binz and Schulz (2022) Reconstructing the Einstellung Effect
finding: A resource-rational model (KL cost to move from prior to policy, prior updated by one gradient step per trial) reproduces the main, DBB, dose, interleaving and time effects.
numbers: Simulated: 90/100 agents used E on C1/C2 and 84/100 on C3/C4 (beta=25, lr=0.5); ablation says all parts are needed. A perfect searcher would check 9261 options; an agent with beta=0.6 checks about 10.
limits: Preprint at time of fetch (journal version in Computational Brain and Behavior 2022). Model fits aggregate percentages only; not tested on new data.
agent_relevance: Gives a mechanism: reuse is cheap, so a cost-aware agent will take it. Predicts that cheaper reasoning budgets give more Einstellung, and that exposure to varied solutions flattens the prior.

source: Bilalic, McLeod, Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts - reality or myth? Cognitive Psychology 56
finding: Chess experts: a familiar solution cut problem solving to the level of players about 3 SD weaker.
numbers: Exp 1 (smothered-mate problem): shorter solution found by 50% of International Masters, 18% of Masters, 0% of Candidate Masters, matching Class A 63%, Class B 13%, Class C 0% on the 1-solution version. Grand Masters 100% on 2-solution. All experts found the short line when the familiar one was disabled.
quote: The presence of a familiar solution reduced the problem solving abilities of the experts to about that of players 3 SDs lower in skill.
limits: Small groups per Elo band. Chess only. Mid-skill experts are hit; top grandmasters are not.
agent_relevance: Fixation is not a knowledge gap: the knowledge was there. So the fix is search control, not more facts (S6).

source: Bilalic, McLeod, Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts
finding: Skill moderates the effect: more expertise means less Einstellung (logistic fit).
numbers: Exp 1: B=.013, Z=8.4, p=.004; 100 Elo points lower cut the odds of finding the short solution by a factor 3.67. Probability found: GM(2550) .64, IM(2450) .32, Master(2350) .12, CM(2150) .01. Exp 2 (four problems): factor 1.82 per 100 points; found .87 at Elo 2500, .67 at 2300, .37 at 2100.
limits: Effect size depends on problem difficulty: on an easier fifth problem all Candidate Masters found the best move. Experts three SD above mean were fooled; five SD above mean mostly not.
agent_relevance: A stronger base model does not remove the effect but may shrink it. Test across model sizes, not one.

source: Bilalic, McLeod, Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts
finding: Experts overestimated their peers' flexibility.
numbers: 12 experts (mean Elo 2231) predicted 86% of IMs, 74% of Masters, 59% of CMs would find the short solution in Exp 1; actual 50%, 18%, 0%. Exp 2 predictions 97/89/73% vs actual 92/69/35%.
limits: Prediction by 12 raters only.
agent_relevance: Self-forecast of flexibility is badly optimistic. An agent's claim that it looked for alternatives should not be trusted without a check (G2, G3).

source: Bilalic, McLeod, Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts (Exp 3)
finding: A plan rejected once stays rejected: fixation can come from a prior rejection, not only a prior success.
numbers: Exp 3 (plan correctly rejected in problem 2, correct again in problem 3 after other changes, 10 minutes per problem): all players failed except one of five Grand Masters; solvers had higher rating (median Elo 2547 vs 2258, Mann-Whitney U=2, p=.017).
limits: Very few top players.
agent_relevance: An operator ruled out earlier in a chain is not reconsidered when the context changes. Log why an option was dropped and re-test when premises change.

source: Bilalic, McLeod, Gobet (2008) Why good thoughts block better ones. Cognition (author manuscript)
finding: Eye movements show the mechanism: attention stays on squares tied to the familiar solution while the player believes they search elsewhere.
numbers: Candidate Masters, two small groups (F df 5,20 imply about 5 per group). 2-solution group: no shift of looking time across six periods (F(5,20)=0.6, ns); 1-solution group moved gaze to the key squares (F(5,20)=11.9, p<.001, partial eta2=.75). None in the 2-solution group found the 3-move mate.
limits: Very small N. Eye data are correlational; one chess problem in Exp 1.
agent_relevance: Search can look like exploring but only re-sample what the first idea predicts. The alternative generator (S6) must be forced away from the first plan's features.

source: Bilalic, McLeod, Gobet (2008) Why good thoughts block better ones
finding: The set lingers after the familiar option is removed: slower even on the problem with only the short solution.
numbers: Exp 1: players who first saw the 2-solution problem took 148 s on the 1-solution problem vs 79 s for fresh players (t(8)=1.67, p=.13, d=1.2). Exp 2: fresh players needed about half the time (t(44)=2.16, p=.036, d=.65); skill by group interaction ns (F(2,40)=0.9).
limits: Exp 1 comparison was not significant; Exp 2 compared across studies, not randomised. Suggestive only.
agent_relevance: A rejected-but-active idea keeps costing time. A fresh restatement (reset) may speed the next try.

source: Bilalic, McLeod, Gobet (2010) The mechanism of the Einstellung (set) effect: a pervasive source of cognitive bias. Current Directions in Psychological Science
finding: Review by the original authors: the first idea directs attention toward consistent information and away from inconsistent; they link this to other biases.
numbers: Restated table: IM 50% vs Class A 63%; Master 18% vs Class B 13%; CM 0% vs Class C 0%. Effect equals about 3 SD of skill. Similar results with a best-solution vs shortest-solution instruction.
limits: Review by the original authors, so it carries their view. The claim that confirmation bias, anchoring and others share one mechanism is hypothesis, not tested.
agent_relevance: Do not build the schema on the one-mechanism-for-all-biases claim.

source: Sheridan and Reingold (2013) The mechanisms and boundary conditions of the Einstellung effect in chess: evidence from eye movements. PLoS ONE 8(10)
finding: Boundary condition: when the familiar move is a blunder, experts avoid it. When it is merely good, experts and novices fall for it equally.
numbers: 17 experts, 17 novices. Problem 1 (Einstellung move advantageous): 8 of 17 experts and 8 of 17 novices chose it. Problems 2-4 (move is a blunder): all experts and most novices avoided it. Experts reached the target region sooner (407 vs 719 ms, t=2.99, p<.01).
limits: Only 4 test problems and 8 fillers. Equal fall-rate of experts and novices in Problem 1 differs from the 2008 skill gradient: a possible failure to reproduce the skill benefit in this setup.
agent_relevance: Fixation needs a decent-looking fallback. A clearly wrong first answer is caught by a check; the danger is the good-enough answer (G3).

source: Sheridan and Reingold (2013)
finding: Experts who found the optimal move disengaged gaze from the Einstellung move over time; those who chose it kept looking at it.
numbers: Experts overall: linear drop in looking at the target region, F(1,66)=13.12, p<.01; novices ns, F(1,66)=2.25. Expertise by time interaction F(3,96)=3.95. Optimal-move experts (n=9) differed from Einstellung-move experts. Most players said they considered the Einstellung move first.
limits: Subset analyses small (9 vs 8 experts).
agent_relevance: Success shows as active disengagement from the first idea. A detector of repeated returns to one candidate could feed the impasse signal (S4).

source: Ellis and Reingold (2014) The Einstellung effect in anagram problem solving: evidence from eye movements. Frontiers in Psychology 5:679
finding: Anagram task: a familiar word as the central string slows solving but speeds encoding.
numbers: N=60 undergraduates, 72 trials, 45 s limit. Overall 52.7% correct, 4.2% wrong, 43.1% timeouts. Response time 15.3 s word vs 13.4 s nonword (t(59)=3.25, p<.01). Accuracy 51.7 vs 53.8%, t(59)=1.52, ns. First-fixation latency on the central string shorter for words (F(1,59)=29.78, p<.001).
limits: Small effect (about 1.9 s); accuracy difference not significant. Mixed pattern of interference and facilitation. Familiarity built into the stimulus, no Luchins-type training.
agent_relevance: Shows the effect needs no long training: a familiar chunk in the prompt can cost time. Familiarity is not purely harmful.

source: Ollinger, Jones, Knoblich (2008) Investigating the effect of mental set on insight problem solving. Experimental Psychology 55(4):269-282
finding: Mental set effects depend on the type of problem in the set (insight sets can help or hurt).
numbers: Three experiments, matchstick tasks. Non-insight problem sets gave no set effect on insight test problems; insight sets gave facilitation or inhibition depending on problem type. Numbers not read.
limits: Abstract seen through search only; do not cite numbers.
agent_relevance: Set effects are specific to similarity between training and test, not general.

source: DeCaro (2016) Inducing mental set constrains procedural flexibility and conceptual understanding in mathematics. Memory and Cognition 44:1138-1148
finding: Mental set induced by problem order in maths equivalence harms strategy flexibility and understanding.
numbers: Two experiments: undergraduates N=41 and fifth-sixth graders N=87 (from a summary page). Complex-first group used the shortcut less, with weaker flexibility and understanding.
limits: Summary page only; effect sizes not checked.
agent_relevance: A cheap design in school maths; the same item set was reused for LLM tests (Haq et al.).

source: Blech, Gaschler, Bilalic (2020) Why do people fail to see simple solutions? Thinking and Reasoning 26(4):552-580
finding: Think-aloud does not change the size of the Einstellung effect in the water-jug task.
numbers: Luchins water-jug design, concurrent verbalisation vs silent: no difference in effect size. Protocols show repeated tries of variants of the old method despite failing. Sample sizes and statistics not seen.
limits: Abstract and index entries only; full text restricted. Not verified.
agent_relevance: Written reasoning mirrors the behaviour in humans; for LLMs the link of written reasoning to the real decision is weaker, so this may not transfer.

source: Bilalic and McLeod (2014) Why your first idea can blind you to a better one. Scientific American
finding: Popular account: expertise helps; active self-reminders and recording contrary facts at once are suggested remedies.
numbers: Eye-tracking study of 5 experts: mean 37 s before they insisted the smothered mate was fastest. Sheridan and Reingold: 17 novices and 17 experts. Advice: remind yourself of the vulnerability; record contrary evidence immediately (Darwin's habit).
limits: Popular-science article; the advice has no measured effect size. Claim that many biases are variants of Einstellung is the authors' view.
agent_relevance: The record-disconfirming-evidence rule matches G2 (cite real output). Untested as an intervention.

source: Haq et al. (2025) Is your LLM trapped in a Mental Set? arXiv 2501.11833
finding: LLMs on Luchins-style maths equivalence items: a tiny test of order effects.
numbers: Items from DeCaro (2016), six complex and six shortcut. Few-shot exact match: Llama-3.1-8B shortcut-only 0.16, shortcut-after-complex 0; Llama-70B 0 and 0.16, complex-then-shortcut 0.66; GPT-4o 0.33, 0.66, 0.66, 0.83. With few-shot plus zero-shot CoT, GPT-4o 0.66-0.83. Steps per correct answer 1 (few-shot) vs 3 (with CoT).
limits: Six items per cell, so one item is 0.17: effects of 0.17 to 0.5 are inside noise. No statistics, no repeats, no no-set control. The reading that 3-step CoT reflects a mental set is not tested.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence. CoT used a 3-step route where one step suffices; this is consistent with cost, not rigidity. Needs a real test with randomised order and many items.

source: Alavi Naeini et al. (2023) Large Language Models are Fixated by Red Herrings. NeurIPS 36 (arXiv 2306.11167)
finding: GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 are fixated by red herrings in Only Connect walls; fewer red herrings gives big gains.
numbers: Humans solved 285/494 walls, 1405/1976 groups. GPT-4 0-shot 6 solved walls, 239 correct groups; GPT-4 5-shot 7 solved, 269 groups. GPT-3.5 0-shot 0 solved, 114 groups. With red herrings removed (OCW-WordNet) GPT-3.5 0-shot reached 337 solved walls and 1522 groups.
limits: Dataset swaps change other things than red herrings (difficulty, word hierarchy). More in-context examples did not help (GPT-3.5 3-shot 140 groups, 10-shot 137). Temperature 0, March 2023 snapshots, now old.
agent_relevance: Distractor-heavy prompts cost a lot, and more examples did not fix it. Removing the distractor beats adding instructions.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Limitations of LLMs in clinical problem-solving arising from inflexible reasoning. arXiv 2502.04381
finding: M-ARC: LLMs fell to medical Einstellung traps; physicians scored higher.
numbers: Most models below 50% on M-ARC, several below 20% (chance level). Best: Gemini-1.5-Pro 50%, o1 48%. Five physicians averaged 66%, SE 5.3%. LLM confidence was high despite low accuracy; larger models better calibrated but still overconfident.
limits: About 100 items; five physicians; the benchmark mixes Einstellung with trick wording and hallucination, so it is not a clean Einstellung measure.
agent_relevance: Fluent confidence without accuracy: stated certainty is no sign the model escaped the habit (G4, G5).

source: Shidara et al. (2026) Advances in LLM reasoning enable flexibility in clinical problem-solving. arXiv 2601.11866
finding: A year later, strong reasoning models reach human level on the same M-ARC traps.
numbers: Reasoning models from OpenAI, Grok, Gemini, Claude, DeepSeek, 15 runs each at highest effort. Claude 4.1 Opus mean 0.751 (95% CI 0.738-0.763). No significant difference from physicians (mean 0.66, CI 0.55-0.75). On the 20 of 100 items most physicians missed, human accuracy was 36%; best model decisively right on 55% (Wilson 90% CI 39.9-80.0).
quote: The top 5 models answered 55% to 70% correctly with high confidence on the human-miss set.
limits: Same item set, possible leakage into training between the two papers; N=100 items. Not a refutation for non-reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Long reasoning-time search cut the medical trap rate a lot. Deliberate alternative search seems to work; the 2025 result depends on model vintage.

source: Chen et al. (2026) MedEinst: Benchmarking the Einstellung Effect in Medical LLMs through Counterfactual Differential Diagnosis. arXiv 2601.06636
finding: MedEinst: stronger models are more fooled by counterfactual traps, not less.
numbers: 5,383 paired cases, 49 diseases, 17 LLMs. GPT-5 base accuracy 54.30% and Gemini-2.5-Pro 53.58%, both with bias trap rates above 50% (Gemini 60.90%). No meaningful correlation between size and robustness. Multi-agent debate frameworks (MDAgent, DyLAN) had robust accuracy about 8-10%.
limits: Cases built and checked by an LLM pipeline; trap rate is conditional (control right, trap wrong). Conflicts with the 2026 M-ARC paper on whether strong models escape.
agent_relevance: Debate and consensus amplify the dominant prior (G4). Supports code-checked selection over voting.

source: Chen et al. (2026) MedEinst
finding: MedEinst mitigation: causal evidence audit plus memory lifts base accuracy and cuts the trap rate on Qwen3-32B.
numbers: Ablation: base 40.25% base acc, 11.86% robust, 43.46% trap rate; plus Dynamic Causal Inference: 55.49 / 19.94 / 38.32; plus memory evolution: 69.49 / 24.21 / 33.75.
limits: Self-reported by the benchmark authors, code not released at the time. Trap rate still one third.
agent_relevance: An evidence-balance step (list for and against) cut trap rate by about 5 points alone and 10 with memory. Needs a fair test of its own.

source: Gu and Shi (2025) Diagnosing shortcut-induced rigidity in continual learning: the Einstellung Rigidity Index. arXiv 2510.00475
finding: Einstellung rigidity index in continual learning of networks: no rigidity found in this setup.
numbers: Two-phase CIFAR-100 with a spurious magenta patch; SGD, EWC, DER++, GPM, DGR. Continual learners reached 0.6 accuracy sooner than scratch (negative adaptation delay); final patched accuracy slightly lower (performance deficit 0.107 +/- 0.039 for the one with positive deficit). Masking the patch helped them, so the patch acted as a distractor.
limits: Authors say the pattern does not show Einstellung; one dataset and backbone. Name borrowed from psychology, not a human-like test.
agent_relevance: Caution against calling any prior-task bias Einstellung. Null result worth keeping.

source: Anonymous abstract (2023) Overcoming the mental set effect in programming problem solving. arXiv 2307.06673 (PPIG 2023)
finding: Programming: two cheap interventions did not break a mental set.
numbers: Two sets of four tasks each with a familiar suboptimal and a better solution. Interventions: unfamiliar editor colour scheme, and an instruction to set aside earlier solutions plus the colour change. Authors report they were insufficient. N not given on the page.
limits: Abstract only. Participant number unknown.
agent_relevance: A plain instruction to forget the earlier solution failed in humans; telling the agent to be flexible in the prompt is not enough.

source: Anonymous abstract (2025) Beware of reasoning overconfidence: pitfalls in the reasoning process for multi-solution tasks. arXiv 2512.01725 (MuSoBench)
finding: Reasoning overconfidence: short chain-of-thought stops at an incomplete solution set; long CoT helps.
numbers: Abstract: short-CoT is overconfident about completeness; long-CoT reduces it through iterative exploration; attention-entropy analysis gives preliminary support for a cognitive-rigidity account. No numbers read.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Convergence on a narrow set of paths is the same failure as Einstellung; longer exploring helps. Matches the 2026 M-ARC result.
